specAnchors.text: understand why a force is exerted on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field and how this effect is applied in simple d.c. electric motors and loudspeakers
describe how the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field changes with the magnitude and direction of the field and current

primer.text: Current plus field equals force: the motor effect pushes a current-carrying wire sideways across a magnetic field, and that push, bent into a coil with a split-ring commutator, becomes the d.c. motor. This note follows the force from a single wire to the spinning coil — including the vertical dead centre — and into the loudspeaker cone.

modules.title: The motor effect on a current-carrying wire
sourceHeadings: Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire
modules.opening: Put a current-carrying wire inside a magnet's field and the two fields fight: the wire's own circular field adds to the field on one side and cancels on the other, leaving a sideways force on the wire. That push is the motor effect, and it is the engine behind d.c. motors and loudspeakers.
keyPoints: A force acts on a current-carrying wire when it sits in a magnetic field.
The effect arises because the wire's field and the magnet's field combine — stronger on one side, weaker on the other.
The force is perpendicular to both the current and the field.
Reversing the current or the field reverses the force direction.
The motor effect is the working principle of d.c. motors and loudspeakers.

low.restatement: Wire with current, dropped between magnet poles, gets shoved sideways. The shove flips if you swap the current's direction or the magnet's poles.
low.analogy: Two crowds pushing a door: reinforcements on one side and defectors on the other swing the door — the wire is the door.
low.examPointer: Name the effect ('the motor effect') AND the mechanism ('the two fields combine') — either alone drops a mark.

medium.restatement: The wire's circular field adds vectorially to the uniform pole field: on one side the circulations reinforce, producing a crowded, strong region; on the other they cancel, leaving a weak region. The unbalanced 'catapult' field exerts the resultant force on the wire, perpendicular to both current and field — reversing either input mirrors the imbalance and flips the force.
medium.analogy: Rowing across a river with a current: your heading plus the flow decides the actual path — flip either and you land on the other bank.
medium.examPointer: For 'explain why a force is exerted', sketch the combined field: crowded on one side, sparse on the other — the sketch is the explanation.

modules.title: Inside the D.C. motor: forces on the horizontal coil
sourceHeadings: Forces on the horizontal coil in a D.C. motor
modules.opening: A d.c. motor is the motor effect bent into a rectangle: a coil of wire between magnet poles. On the horizontal sides the currents run in opposite directions, so the left-hand rule gives one side an upward force and the other a downward force — a turning couple that spins the coil.
keyPoints: A d.c. motor uses a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
The two horizontal sides carry currents in opposite directions.
The motor effect gives one side an upward force and the other a downward force.
The opposite forces form a couple that rotates the coil about its axle.
A split-ring commutator reverses the coil's current every half turn to keep the rotation going.

low.restatement: Current goes up one side of the coil and down the other. Between the poles, one side is pushed up and the other down — the coil spins like a key turning.
low.analogy: Two children on opposite sides of a roundabout, one pushing up, one pushing down on the far rail — the platform turns.
low.examPointer: Say 'a couple' or 'opposite forces on the two sides' — writing 'the magnet spins the coil' has no mechanism in it.

medium.restatement: Each horizontal side is a current-carrying wire in the field, so each feels a force perpendicular to both current and field; with antiparallel currents the forces are antiparallel, producing torque about the axle. The split-ring commutator re-aligns the current with the poles every half turn, so the torque never changes sign and rotation is sustained.
medium.analogy: A commutator is a smarter reverse gear: it flips your pedalling direction exactly when the crank passes dead centre, so the wheel never stalls.
medium.examPointer: For 6-mark motor explanations, chain: opposite currents → opposite forces → couple → rotation → commutator sustains it. Miss a link, lose a mark.

modules.title: Half a turn: the vertical coil and the flipped coil
sourceHeadings: Forces on the coil when rotated 180°
modules.opening: Two special positions test the motor's cleverness. With the coil vertical, the two sides sit at the top and bottom where their forces no longer form a couple — the split ring chooses that moment to swap the current. Half a turn later the sides have swapped places, and without the commutator the forces would now push the coil backwards.
keyPoints: With the coil vertical, the forces on the sides act towards the axle and produce no turning effect.
The split-ring commutator swaps the current contacts exactly at the vertical position.
After a 180° rotation, each side has moved to where the other was.
Without the commutator, the forces after half a turn would oppose the rotation and hold the coil still.
With the commutator, the current reversal keeps the forces driving the same rotational sense.

low.restatement: Coil upright: the pushes now squeeze the coil instead of turning it — that is when the commutator swaps the wires. Half a turn on, the sides have traded places, and the swapped current makes their pushes still drive the spin.
low.analogy: Rowers switching stroke sides exactly as the boat crosses dead centre — the swap keeps the boat spinning in one direction.
low.examPointer: Vertical-position questions want 'no turning effect' — the forces still exist; they just act through the axle line.

medium.restatement: At the vertical orientation each side's force is radial — collinear with the axle plane — so the torque arm is zero and the couple vanishes. The 180° problem is geometric: side currents have swapped their field-relative positions, so a constant current would give forces opposing the established rotation; the commutator's synchronized reversal re-aligns current with position, restoring the driving couple.
medium.analogy: A film projector's shutter flips each frame at the exact blackout moment — the swap is invisible in the motion but essential to the story.
medium.examPointer: Draw the 180° coil and mark forces BOTH with and without the commutator: the contrast earns the explanation mark.

modules.title: Loudspeakers and the levers of magnetic force
modules.opening: A loudspeaker is the motor effect turned into sound: a coil carrying the audio current sits in a radial field, and the force on it — reversing with every swing of the current — drives the cone in and out. The same physics answers the control question: force grows with current and with field strength, and flips when either is flipped.
keyPoints: A loudspeaker coil sits in a magnetic field and carries the audio current.
The motor-effect force moves the coil and cone in and out along the axis.
The current's direction reverses with the alternating signal, so the force alternates too.
The force grows with the size of the current and the strength of the magnetic field.
The force reverses when either the current or the field direction is reversed.

low.restatement: Music current flows through the speaker coil; the field pushes the coil and cone out, the current reverses, the push pulls the cone in. The cone's vibrations are the sound you hear.
low.analogy: The cone is a drum skin played by an invisible finger that taps out, in, out, in — following the music's signal exactly.
low.examPointer: Link the alternating current to the alternating force explicitly — 'the cone vibrates at the frequency of the signal' is the mark.

medium.restatement: The loudspeaker geometry puts the coil in a radial field so the motor-effect force is always axial: force magnitude scales with current and field, direction follows the instantaneous current sense. The cone therefore reproduces the waveform — displacement tracking the signal — and louder output comes from larger current swings or stronger fields.
medium.analogy: The radial field is a curved slide: whatever direction the coil pushes, the slide converts it into the same in-out motion of the cone.
medium.examPointer: For 6.14 phrasing: the force increases with field strength and with current, and reverses when EITHER is reversed — quote all three clauses.

glossary.definition: The force experienced by a current-carrying wire when it lies in a magnetic field.
The contact that reverses the coil's current every half turn of a d.c. motor.
A pair of opposite forces on opposite sides of an axle that turns a coil.

workedExample.prompt: A d.c. motor is set up as shown in the diagram. Determine whether the coil rotates clockwise or anticlockwise when viewed from the position shown, and explain your reasoning.
steps: Identify the current direction along each side of the coil from the supply connections in the diagram.
Identify the magnetic field direction between the poles, from north to south.
Apply the left-hand rule to each horizontal side: first finger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb gives the force.
One side is pushed up and the other down, so the coil turns; reading the diagram, the side with the force towards the viewer determines the rotation sense as anticlockwise from the viewpoint shown.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The coil rotates anticlockwise as viewed in the diagram, because the left-hand rule gives opposite vertical forces on the two sides of the coil.
